title: Noah Centineo & Andrew Koji Ignite 'Street Fighter' Buzz: First Reactions from The Hollywood Reporter
body:
The buzz surrounding Paramount Pictures’ upcoming “Street Fighter” is already louder than the roar of a Shadaloo battle arena. With a cast that pairs teen‑heartthrob Noah Centineo with martial‑arts veteran Andrew Koji, director Kitao Sakurai’s live‑action rendition of Capcom’s legendary fighting franchise is slated to hit theaters on October 16. Early screenings have generated a wave of reactions that suggest the film will deliver a blend of nostalgic fan service and unapologetically over‑the‑top entertainment, positioning it as the next big “dumb‑fun” blockbuster of the summer‑to‑fall slate.

Sakurai, best known for his work on the “Mortal Kombat” reboot, approached the project with an eye toward honoring the source material while also embracing the comic‑book‑ish absurdity that has long defined the video‑game series. The result, according to the first wave of audience feedback, is a kaleidoscopic visual feast that leans heavily into the neon‑lit aesthetic of the 1990s arcade era. From the flamboyant costumes of characters like Sagat and Cammy to the hyper‑stylized fight choreography, the film appears to have spared no expense in recreating the game’s iconic moments. Viewers praised the production design for its fidelity to the original pixel‑art palette, noting that the set pieces—particularly the bustling streets of Metro City and the eerie, rain‑soaked rooftops of Shadaloo’s headquarters—evoke the same adrenaline‑pumping vibe that made the arcade cabinets a cultural touchstone.

The casting choices have become a focal point of discussion. Centineo, who rose to fame through rom‑com fare such as “To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before,” steps into the role of the charismatic yet conflicted protagonist, a departure that many see as a calculated gamble to draw a broader, younger audience. Koji, celebrated for his martial‑arts prowess in “The Man with the Iron Fists” and the Netflix series “Warrior,” assumes the mantle of the stoic, battle‑hardened Ryu. Critics have noted that the chemistry between the two leads is surprisingly effective, with Koji’s disciplined combat style providing a grounding counterpoint to Centineo’s more playful, improvisational energy. Supporting roles, filled by a mix of seasoned genre actors and fresh faces, further enrich the ensemble, delivering punchy one‑liners that echo the game’s trademark humor.

While the film’s tone leans heavily into camp, it does not entirely abandon narrative depth. Early reactions indicate that the screenplay attempts to weave a modest origin story for the rivalry between Ryu and the series’ primary antagonist, M. Bison, while also exploring themes of personal honor and the consequences of unchecked power. However, some reviewers caution that the plot may feel secondary to the spectacle, warning that audiences seeking a tightly woven storyline might be left wanting. Nonetheless, the consensus among those who have seen the preview is that the movie’s primary objective is to entertain, not to reinvent the franchise, and it largely succeeds on that front.

From an industry perspective, “Street Fighter” arrives at a moment when studios are eager to capitalize on the resurgence of video‑game adaptations, a trend sparked by the success of titles like “Sonic the Hedgehog” and “Uncharted.” Paramount’s investment signals confidence that the brand’s global recognition can translate into box‑office returns, especially when paired with a release window that avoids direct competition from other major franchises. Moreover, the film’s marketing strategy—leveraging social media challenges, retro arcade pop‑up events, and collaborations with gaming influencers—suggests a concerted effort to engage both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

Looking ahead, the October 16 debut will be a litmus test for how far studios can push the envelope of fan‑driven cinema without alienating mainstream audiences. If the initial enthusiasm translates into strong ticket sales, it could pave the way for a more ambitious slate of video‑game adaptations, possibly even spawning sequels or spin‑offs that delve deeper into the rich lore of the “Street Fighter” universe. For now, the film stands as a promise of high‑octane, nostalgic escapism—a reminder that sometimes, the most enjoyable movies are the ones that unabashedly celebrate their own absurdity.
